thread.title: Chip Stocks Look To Find Bottom In Early 2019 | Investor's Business Daily

author: PATRICK SEITZ
title: Chip Stocks Look To Find Bottom In Early 2019 | Investor's Business Daily
text:
It's a bad time for chip stocks, and things aren't likely to improve in the semiconductor sector for a couple of quarters, analysts say.
X Many chip companies warned about sales and earnings heading into the December quarter. Wall Street now is anxious to hear not only about fourth-quarter results from those companies but also their guidance for the first quarter and full year 2019.
So late January will be a critical period for chip stocks, as companies begin to report fourth-quarter results and give their outlooks for the year ahead.
"The semi sector won't see stabilization for at least another quarter," Rosenblatt Securities analyst Hans Mosesmann told Investor's Business Daily. The hope is that March-quarter guidance will be the last downward revision before the chip sector resets, he said.

Please contact customer service CLOSE Sales Reverting To The Mean "We went through a couple of years where the semi companies had been growing at double-digit rates, and that's not the normalized growth rate," Mosesmann said. "You just can't grow at that pace for a long period of time. There has to be a reversion to the mean. That mean is 4%, 5% or 6% growth."
In 2019, semiconductor industry sales are likely to be flat or down 5%, he said.
The performance of chip stocks also has implications for the broader stock market. That's because it's unusual for there to be a stock market rally without semiconductor stocks participating.
"Semis are a leading indicator for general economic activity," Susquehanna Financial Group analyst Christopher Rolland told IBD. That's why semiconductor stocks usually lead downturns, he said. Before the current downturn, the last one was in 2011, he said.
Rolland describes the current downturn as "modest" but broad-based. It hit the memory-chip sector hardest. Graphics processors are experiencing a hangover from the boom and bust in cryptocurrency mining. Sales of smartphones, especially Apple 's ( AAPL ) new iPhone models, have been sluggish, hurting chip suppliers. Automotive and industrial chip markets also have weakened, he said.
"It's tough times in semis right now," he said. "The market is getting hit on all sides."
Bright Spots Among Chip Stocks Still, analysts see bright spots among chip stocks.
Mosesmann likes Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) for possible market share gains from Intel ( INTC ) in personal computers and servers. He also favors Nvidia ( NVDA ) because it provides a "building-block" technology for next-generation data centers, artificial intelligence and autonomous driving.
Plus, Xilinx ( XLNX ) is well-positioned in data centers and 5G wireless base stations, Mosesmann said.
Rolland sees Xilinx and Mellanox Technologies ( MLNX ) as winners based on secular trends. Xilinx is a player in artificial intelligence. Mellanox is a likely acquisition target, he said.
This chip sector downturn is a little different from ones in years past, Mosesmann said. It has come in waves, based on market segments, and is more muted than prior cycles, he said. Mosesmann is looking for one or two more quarters of volatility before the chip sector stabilizes.
Analysts will be watching inventories and production lead times for signs that the market is bottoming.
IBD's Electronics-Semiconductor Manufacturing industry group currently ranks No. 149 out of 197 groups. The Semiconductor Fabless industry group ranks No. 73.
Micron Latest Chipmaker To Disappoint Late Thursday, Micron Technology ( MU ) offered a dreary outlook for memory-chip sales in the near term. The news sent its stock to its lowest level since August 2017.
Micron warned about an oversupply in DRAM markets, including data centers. It also said Nand flash memory-chip inventories remain elevated. The company characterized the downturn as an "air pocket" and said it expects memory-chip demand to reaccelerate in the second half of 2019.
Micron delivered mixed results for its fiscal first quarter ended Nov. 29 with earnings beating views but sales coming up short. For the current quarter, Micron guided to earnings of $1.75 per share on sales of $6 billion. Wall Street was modeling adjusted earnings per share of $2.44 on sales of $7.34 billion, according to Thomson Reuters.
Baby, We Can't See The Bottom In a report Tuesday, Morgan Stanley chip analysts said the bottom for the chip market is not yet in sight.
"It's going to get worse before it gets better, as weaker end demand and inventory reductions drive negative estimate revisions," they said.
The investment bank sees semiconductor revenue declining 5% next year to about $446 billion, mostly due to memory chips. Excluding memory, it expects chip revenue to climb 2% to about $315 billion in 2019.
"It's too early to call the bottom," Morgan Stanley said. "Certainly there was some weakness signaled in the Q4 outlooks, but the real impact to earnings is still ahead."
